spans.s:
Ugra in one passage of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka upaniṣad seems to have a technical force, denoting ‘man in authority,’ or according to Max Müller's rendering, ‘policeman.’ Roth compares a passage in the Rigveda, where, however, the word has simply the general sense of ‘mighty man.’ Bo7htlingk, in his rendering of the upaniṣad, treats the word as merely adjectival.
Foot notes iv. 3, 37. 38.
St. Petersburg Dictionary, s.v.
vii. 38, 6.

Ugra-deva is mentioned with turvaśa and yadu in the Rigveda apparently as a powerful protector. The name occurs also in the pañcaviṃśa brāhmaṇa and the taittirīya Āraṇyaka, where he is styled rājani and called a leper (kilāsa).
Foot notes i. 36, 18 (Ugrādeva).
xiv. 3, 17; xxiii. 16, 11.
v. 4, 12.
Cf. Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 147; Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, s.v., who suggests that in the Rv. passage the word should be taken adjectivally.

Ugra-sena is mentioned in the Śatapatha brāhmaṇa (xiii. 5, 4, 3), and in a gāthā there cited as being, with bhīmasena and śrutasena, a Pārikṣitīya and a brother of janamejaya. The brothers were cleansed by the horse sacrifice from sin.
